next_steps: Share initial per-token cost model spreadsheet
Draft proposed 6-week pilot SOW and timeline
action_items: Carlos: circulate cost model with assumptions by 2025-08-10
Priya: prepare staging benchmark run plan and VM/GPU config by 2025-08-11

meeting_header: 2025-08-07 | 16:00 PDT | Duration: 52m | Attendees: Carlos (Redwood AE), Priya (Redwood SE), Jared (Elysian), Marta (Elysian), Anika (Elysian)
summary: POC scoping to validate per-token economics for Elysian's conversational shopping assistant. Discussed workload sizing (QPS & token distribution), target latency SLOs, batching/caching knobs, benchmark plan and 6-week pilot timeline. Action items assigned for cost model, benchmarks, and security docs.
topics: workload sizing; per-token cost modeling; batching/caching strategy; benchmark plan; pilot timeline; security & VPC; success criteria
transcript:
[00:00] Carlos: Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick agenda — go through your workload, walk through economics, then outline benchmarks and pilot timeline. sound good?
[00:12] Jared: Yeah that's perfect. thanks. we've been wanting to nail down the unit economics before we commit to a reserved capacity.
[00:18] Priya: Great. maybe to start — Marta, can you give the traffic profile you mentioned in the form? qps, peak windows, token distributions?
[00:24] Marta: Yep. rough numbers: normal day ~120 qps across 3 services, peak up to 380 qps during promos. median request length is short — about 30 tokens for chat snippets, but about 12% of calls are long context retrievals ~700 tokens. average response tokens per request around 45.
[00:45] Anika: to add, our shopping assistant also does embedding-based rerank for product recs — that's a separate flow but will hit the same model infra for small jobs. expect ~15k embeddings/day.
[00:55] Carlos: Good, that's helpful. for costing we typically split generation and embedding units — embeddings are charged per vector op; generation is per-token.
[01:04] Jared: We're trying to stay within a monthly budget of about $25k for inference to start. we can flex if the uplift is clear but wanted to set that guardrail.
[01:14] Priya: Understood. a couple of knobs that impact per-token: batching window (latency trade), prefix/KV caching for repeated contexts, and model quantization. If you can tolerate a 10–30ms additional P95 we'd batch more aggressively and cut token cost.
[01:28] Marta: our p95 latency goal for the assistant is 350ms end-to-end. Is that feasible with batching?
[01:34] Priya: Yes, with small-ish batches and async prefix caching we can stay under 350ms p95 for most flows. heavy long-context cases will be higher — that's where a fallback to a larger memory-optimized variant might help.
[01:46] Jared: Walk me through the per-token math — we ran a quick internal calc but the numbers vary a lot depending on GPU and batching.
[01:54] Carlos: Sure, high level: cost_per_token = infra_cost_per_hour / (tokens_per_hour_served). infra cost per hour depends on instance type and utilization. for example, on an A100-style node with our optimized runtime you might see effective cost of $0.15–0.28 per 1k tokens depending on batching and quantization. that translates to $0.00015–0.00028 per token.
[02:14] Jared: So at 120 qps avg and 45 tokens per call that's roughly X tokens/day? (math sounds)
[02:20] Marta: we did a quick calc — ~466k tokens/hour at 120 qps * 45 tokens = 540k tokens/hr? wait hold on, math slip.
[02:29] Anika: (laughs) we have spreadsheets. I'll send the export.
[02:33] Priya: no worries, we'll take the raw traces. for the POC benchmark we'll run through realistic RPS ramps and token histograms you provide. that gives us a measured cost per token under your distribution.
[02:44] Jared: timeline expectation? we want results fast — ideally a 2-week benchmark phase and then a 4–6 week pilot.
[02:51] Carlos: That's reasonable. our standard: Week0 = kickoff + access + infra prep; Week1 = benchmark runs (staging); Week2 = analyze + optimize batching/caching; Week3–8 = pilot in dedicated or hosted with production traffic mirror.
[03:05] Anika: Access — we prefer private deployment in our VPC for compliance reasons. can you run in our VPC?
[03:10] Priya: Yes. Redwood Private supports VPC deployments; we'll need network peering details and a service account. We'll also share our KMS integration notes.
[03:18] Marta: And SOC2? we need audit logs and RBAC for this pilot.
[03:22] Carlos: We have SOC2 Type II. we'll attach the pack. audit logs and per-token tracing available in Console; role-based controls supported via SSO/SAML.
[03:33] Jared: One concern — your per-token estimates assume certain utilization. if our bursts are spiky, that can blow up hourly costs. what mitigations exist?
[03:43] Priya: Good question. multiple mitigations: configure burst autoscaling with caps, use cheaper model variants for non-critical paths, add prefix caching for repeated session tokens, and reserved capacity if you want deterministic unit cost. For spikes, we can implement a fallback tier (lower-cost model) to keep latency bounded while saving cost.
[04:00] Marta: For our catalog re-rank flows, we could offload embeddings to a separate cheaper host to avoid touching the main generation cluster.
[04:06] Carlos: Yep — we often recommend pushing embeddings to a dedicated scaler or batch job. that reduces cross-contamination on the generation pool.
[04:13] Anika: What about quantization — how much does INT8 or 4-bit move the needle?
[04:18] Priya: In our benchmarks, moving from FP16 to 4-bit quant reduced token compute by ~30–45% depending on model architecture and sequence length; throughput improved, P95 latency slightly better in many cases but worst-case long context generation may get CPU-bound memory tradeoffs. We'll include quant profiles in the benchmark matrix.
[04:35] Jared: Are there limits on function calling/structured output that change costs? our assistant emits JSON payloads and sometimes calls out to external tools.
[04:43] Priya: Function calls are still generation tokens — but we can reduce cost by schema-constraining responses and using short function args. Also streaming or chunked outputs can help reduce blocking latency. We'll test those patterns.
[04:55] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[05:00] Carlos: Let's be explicit on success criteria — what would make this POC a go/no-go for Elysian?
[05:06] Jared: For us: 1) <=350ms p95 for main shopping assistant flow at 90% of traffic; 2) cost <= $0.10 per 1k tokens on average across month-one traffic (that's our internal target); 3) security signoffs (SOC2 + VPC + KMS). If those three are green, we'll move to reserved capacity negotiation.
[05:25] Priya: Good clear targets. We'll aim the benchmark to validate p95 and effective cost per 1k tokens. We'll also provide a sensitivity table showing cost at different utilization/batch windows.
[05:36] Marta: For acceptance, we also want a simple anomaly detection — whether quality regressions happen when using quantized models. can you run side-by-side evals?
[05:44] Priya: Absolutely. we'll do quality evals (prompt sets you provide) and compare outputs across FP16, 8-bit and 4-bit variants. we'll report BLEU-ish / embedding-similarity metrics and a human sample review.
[05:56] Carlos: Ok, benchmark plan at a high level: collect traces (you provide), prepare staging cluster in your VPC or our staging, run 3 x 2-hour load tests at different concurrency and token mixes, measure cost, latency, token/sec, and cache hit rates. then optimize batching windows and cache TTLs.
[06:14] Anika: For data — can we mask PII? we'll scrub user identifiers in traces.
[06:19] Priya: Yes please, we only need sequence lengths and token histograms and example prompts — scrub sensitive fields.
[06:25] Jared: About budget — if pilot shows we need $40k/month to meet latency we might still proceed but want to know tradeoffs — can you provide a table: cost vs latency vs quality?
[06:34] Carlos: We'll include a decision matrix: rows by model variant/quantization, columns cost per 1k tokens, p95 latency, and an estimated quality delta. that's part of the deliverable.
[06:45] Marta: Any caveats about embedding charges? we run a batch reindex nightly.
[06:49] Priya: Batch embedding jobs are cheap per vector but can spike I/O. We'll recommend running those on a separate scheduler and provide per-embedding cost estimate in the spreadsheet.
[06:58] Jared: Ok last: timeline and signoffs. you said Week0 kickoff — can we aim to start Aug 18th?
[07:04] Carlos: Yes that gives us time to get network info and an SSO test user. so kickoff 2025-08-18, benchmarks 8/19–8/25, analysis 8/26–8/29, pilot starting 9/2.
[07:15] Anika: Works for me.
[07:17] Carlos: Great. I'll send the cost-model template with assumptions and a link to the benchmark spreadsheet. Priya will post the detailed runbook.
[07:24] Priya: I'll include GPU types, batch windows to test (0ms, 10ms, 25ms), cache TTLs (session vs global) and a plan to compare FP16/8/4.
[07:34] Jared: Thanks everyone. we'll get the traces and stakeholder list over.
[07:37] Marta: I'll also attach our network diagram and compliance contacts.
[07:40] Carlos: Perfect. recap in the notes: deliver cost spreadsheet, schedule benchmark, share SOC2 and network diagrams, produce pilot SOW. Any other items?
[07:49] Jared: Not from me. thanks.
[07:51] Carlos: Ok meeting adjourned.
[07:54] (call ends)
